svg.text: When NOT to Use Optional: The 5 Anti-Patterns
Brian Goetz's rule: Use Optional as a shield on return values, never as a burden on fields or inputs

g.text: 1. NEVER Use as Class/DTO Fields
❌ private Optional<String> email;
• Not Serializable: Breaks Redis caching, network transfers.
• Jackson JSON issue: creates nested {"email": {"present": true}}.
✔ Fix: Keep field raw String; wrap at getter: getEmail() -> Optional
2. NEVER Use as Method Parameters
❌ public void save(Optional<User> user)
• Forces callers to wrap values: save(Optional.of(u)) or Optional.empty().
• Pollutes caller code and violates API ergonomics.
✔ Fix: Accept raw type, use method overloading or null checks inside.
3. NEVER Put Inside Collections
❌ List<Optional<User>> or Map<String, Optional<V>>
• Collections already represent 0 to N items naturally.
• Storing empty containers causes double-looping and double-unpacking.
✔ Fix: Use empty List / Map, or filter with flatMap(Optional::stream).
4. NEVER Return null From Optional Methods
❌ public Optional<User> find() { return null; }
• The ultimate betrayal: violates the guarantee of safety to callers.
• Caller chaining opt.map(...) will immediately crash with NPE!
✔ Fix: Always return Optional.empty() when value is absent.
5. Low-Level DAO vs Service Layer Consideration
SQL NULL ➔ JDBC Java null (Contract: ResultSet.getString() returns null)
• In low-level JDBC DAO queries, converting every column to Optional adds object allocation overhead.
• Architectural Rule: Keep low-level data layer direct. Introduce Optional at the Service Layer / Domain Boundary
where business logic decides what to present to clients and callers.
✔ Summary: Use Optional as a RETURN TYPE at API boundaries and service layer methods.
